title: Zelensky Lands in Istanbul to Map a November Summit, Beijing Expands Coast Guard Patrols East of Taiwan, and Syria Asks About Joining the Makkah Bloc
subhead: Three of the four tracks that matter this week moved on the same weekend: Ukraine's diplomacy hardened into a concrete trilateral timetable, China began treating Taiwan's eastern approaches as a routine enforcement space, and Damascus opened the door to the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani security pact. In Tehran, diplomacy and a strike package are running in parallel.

sections.heading: Istanbul, Abu Dhabi or Geneva: Ukraine's Talks Get a Date
sections.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Istanbul on Saturday at President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's invitation, his office confirmed on Telegram, for talks covering Black Sea shipping security, bilateral defence cooperation and the diplomatic track toward ending the war (Kyiv Post, Oct 31). The trip carries an operational edge: it followed drone attacks that sank a container ship off Bulgaria and killed roughly two dozen seafarers, according to Kyiv Post's reporting, which is why maritime protection rather than summit choreography topped the agenda.

The timing matters more than the venue. Ankara is now preparing working-level trilateral talks between Ukrainian, US and Russian delegations, with Abu Dhabi and Switzerland under consideration as hosts, and Zelensky's team hopes to convene between Nov 6 and Nov 10, subject to Washington's confirmation (Kyiv Post). Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov has said Moscow is prepared to resume trilateral talks after Russia's Nov 4 National Unity Day holiday, and characterized the coming session as exploratory.

Do not overread the momentum. Three things constrain it. First, both sides have described the next round as preparatory, not substantive. Second, Erdogan's leverage runs through Washington: Ankara told Trump in a recent call that it was ready to help revive formal negotiations, but the sequencing and content are still set by Moscow and the White House. Third, the week has produced contradictory US signals on Ukraine — a State Department approval of a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defence interceptors, announced Friday at the G20 in Atlanta, sitting alongside a decision to waive fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limit logistical and intelligence assistance (Associated Press).
sections.whyItMatters: A date on a calendar is the first concrete deliverable of the autumn diplomatic push. If the Nov 6-10 window holds, it will be the first trilateral contact since the US posture toward Kyiv shifted, and the Black Sea agenda gives both sides something to trade that is not territory.

sections.heading: Beijing Calls the Waters East of Taiwan Its Enforcement Zone
sections.body:
China's Coast Guard said on Oct 31 that a flotilla led by its Hulishi vessel conducted a 'routine law enforcement patrol' in the waters east of Taiwan, part of what state media described as stepped-up control of the area through October (People's Daily, Nov 1). Taiwan's Coast Guard rejected the claim outright, saying two Chinese ships were involved, that its own vessels were sent to monitor, and that Beijing's attempt to 'harass ships at sea through radio communications' was an unlawful expansion of power that undermines regional peace (Reuters, via The Straits Times).

Taipei's reading is that this is blockade rehearsal using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets — and the eastern seaboard is precisely the space it considers critical to wartime resupply from allies. The same weekend brought a second signal: China sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands at the top of the South China Sea, and Taiwan says it has 'expelled' Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times in 2026 (Reuters). The Pratas sit more than 400km from Taiwan, with no permanent civilian population, which is exactly why analysts regard them as the easiest target and the hardest to defend.

The qualitative shift is bureaucratic rather than kinetic. China is building a record of routine enforcement east of the island and around Pratas, so that presence becomes the baseline rather than an escalation. That is harder to reverse than a single exercise.
sections.whyItMatters: Patrols east of Taiwan test the resupply corridor that any defence of the island depends on, and this weekend's parallel move near Pratas extends the same logic into the South China Sea. It also lands days before APEC's leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov 18-19, giving Beijing a claim of normalcy to defend in the room.

sections.heading: The Quad Reassembles Around Chokepoints, Not Around China
sections.body:
On the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his counterparts from Australia, India and Japan on Saturday — the Quad format — before chairing the closing session on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red, Black and South China seas (Associated Press). Rubio's public framing was trade, not deterrence: 'secure supply chains are essential for growth,' he posted on X, adding that Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb 'must remain secure and open to commerce' (AP). A joint statement issued after the Asia-Pacific talks referenced 'Super Intelligence' six times, with a footnote clarifying that in Australia, India and Japan the term refers to artificial intelligence — the phrase Trump adopted at the UN General Assembly.

Read the substance past the footnote. The Quad's public output this weekend was about maritime insurance risk and critical minerals, not about Taiwan or the South China Sea as military problems. That is partly a function of the G20 setting, where the US presidency deliberately narrowed the agenda to energy security and supply chain resilience, and partly a hedge: India and Japan both carry heavy exposure to Gulf energy flows, and neither wants a communique that forecloses the option of working with Beijing on minerals.
sections.whyItMatters: Chokepoint security has become the lowest-common-denominator agenda for the Indo-Pacific grouping, which tells you how much of the region's strategic anxiety is now maritime and economic rather than territorial. It also explains why the Quad could meet productively in the same city where the G20 could not produce a communique at all.

sections.heading: Atlanta Produced No Communique, and That Was the Plan
sections.body:
The G20 foreign ministers' meeting closed on Oct 31 without a joint communique. The US presidency issued a chair's statement instead — a seven-paragraph document covering energy security, supply chain resilience and 'geopolitical tensions' that names no country, accuses no one, and records no agreement (G20 Chair's Statement, Atlanta, Oct 31). Rubio was blunt at his closing press conference: 'I wouldn't pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems' (AP).

The mechanics were messier than the language. Rubio canceled the traditional group photo after European diplomats objected to standing alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and threatened to boycott it. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, attending his first G20 as a guest, said the outcome was unsurprising: 'We have wars going on, and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it's very difficult to agree on a common line' (AP). Diplomats cited divisions over Ukraine, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and Chinese activity in the South China Sea — and also over the administration's decision not to invite G20 member South Africa.

Two details are worth keeping. The chair's statement does contain one substantive new norm: a call for the G20 to agree that food and agricultural products 'should not be used as a tool for economic or political coercion.' And the document looks forward explicitly to the leaders' summit in Miami and to the UK presidency in 2027 — meaning Washington is treating Miami as the real event and Atlanta as a procedural warm-up.
sections.whyItMatters: A G20 that cannot sign a paragraph on Ukraine or Iran while Russia sits at the table has stopped functioning as a crisis-management forum. The Miami summit in December now carries the burden, and the US has pre-committed to a low-ambition format.

sections.heading: In Tehran, a Two-Day Hormuz Plan Sits Beside a Strike Package
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Sunday that talks are under way with Qatari mediators on a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US accepts Tehran's conditions (Al Jazeera, Nov 1). Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said he had reviewed a letter from Vice President JD Vance and that Washington's tone had 'changed completely' — a 'very positive sign.' Reuters reported that Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha on Saturday, following more than 12 hours of Iran-Qatar discussions in Tehran on Friday, with the talks coordinated in regular contact with Washington. A source briefed on the negotiations said Qatar had brought a seven-day, step-by-step trust-building proposal a week earlier that Tehran did not find satisfactory; Iran has been pushing its own seven-day plan since September, which requires the US to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed Hormuz route before the strait reopens.

Against that, the coercive track is intact. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei issued a statement on Saturday ordering the armed forces to prepare for any attack, declaring that 'any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response' (Reuters). Rezaei said Tehran is debating whether to lift its long-standing ban on nuclear weapons if hostilities resume, while stressing no decision had been taken. Rubio, in Atlanta, said Trump has not decided on new strikes but would prefer a diplomatic solution, and that contacts with Iran 'have actually never stopped.' AP has reported that US officials have told Middle East allies to be prepared for potential renewed strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections, and for possible Iranian retaliation (AP, via CNBC).
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between a two-day reopening plan and a geographically unrestricted retaliation doctrine is the whole story. Both tracks are live because both sides are using the other as leverage — and the midterm vote on Tuesday is the switch that changes the calculation.

sections.heading: Damascus Circles a Defence Pact It Cannot Yet Afford to Join
sections.body:
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said on Saturday that 'discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance,' speaking at the IISS Manama Dialogue in Bahrain (Daily Sabah, AFP). The Makkah pact, signed on Aug 7 by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all three, and provides for intelligence sharing, joint exercises, counterterrorism coordination and defence-industrial cooperation. It has a permanent secretariat in Riyadh, and Pakistan's retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood as its first secretary-general. Membership is open to others with the unanimous approval of the founding three.

No formal application has been made. The pact itself is still maturing: Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have completed ratification, while Türkiye's domestic approval process is still running. Its first operational test came in October, when renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi targets prompted an emergency meeting in Riyadh at which members agreed to deploy previously agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia as collective defence.

Syria's interest follows President Ahmed al-Sharaa's Oct 6 visit to Riyadh and al-Shibani's late-August trip to Islamabad, the first by a Syrian foreign minister in nearly two decades. Syrian officials have denied reports that Damascus would provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia, insisting cooperation runs through bilateral channels. The real driver is reconstruction: a state rebuilding its armed forces after Assad's collapse needs a security guarantor and a defence-industrial supplier, and the Makkah bloc offers both without requiring the force commitments NATO-style membership would imply.
sections.whyItMatters: A Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani mutual defence bloc adding Syria would extend a Sunni-majority security architecture from the Gulf to the Levant, covering three of the region's live fronts. It also gives Damascus an alternative to dependence on a single patron while it rebuilds — a shift worth watching far more closely than its public diplomacy suggests.

bottomLine: This weekend moved three tracks forward and one sideways. Ukraine got a target date — Nov 6 to Nov 10 for trilateral working-level talks, with Istanbul having served as the staging ground — even as Washington simultaneously approved $2.1bn in Patriot interceptors and softened its pressure on Moscow. China formalized routine Coast Guard enforcement east of Taiwan and near Pratas, converting a periodic show of force into an administrative fact. Syria began openly weighing membership in the Makkah defence pact, which would join the Levant to a Gulf security structure. And the G20, meeting in Atlanta, produced no communique at all — a chair's statement that names no country and commits to nothing, with the group's real test deferred to Miami in December. On Iran, diplomacy and the strike option are running on parallel tracks and neither has been closed: Qatar is mediating a two-day Hormuz reopening, Tehran's leadership has ordered a geographically unrestricted response to any attack, and US allies have been told to expect possible strikes after Tuesday's midterms.
